title: Eavesdropping on Silence: How Submarine Internet Cables Can Now Detect Whales Without a Sound
summary: Whales are the ocean's loudmouths—their songs can travel thousands of kilometers. But here's the catch: they spend most of their time in silence. For conservationists tracking how climate change and human activity are reshaping whale migration, that silence is a huge blind spot. Now, researchers in Norway have found a way to listen with light. Robin Rørstadbotnen and Martin Landrø at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) have adapted a technique called distributed acoustic sensing (DAS). DAS fires laser pulses through undersea fiber-optic cables—the same ones that carry your internet. Tiny imperfections in the fiber scatter some light back. When an acoustic wave (like a whale call) strains the cable, it shifts the phase of that backscattered light. Scientists can read those shifts to pinpoint sounds. But Rørstadbotnen and Landrø wondered: could DAS detect not just sound, but the physical wake of a swimming whale? As a whale moves, it generates hydrodynamic pressure and velocity fields—ultra-low-frequency signals similar to those of a passing ship. The duo revisited data from a seabed cable off Svalbard, in the Norwegian Arctic. By filtering for specific frequencies and analyzing how signals varied along the cable's length, they could identify ships up to 550 meters away and at depths of 413 meters. Crucially, they also distinguished silent whales swimming within 40 meters of the cable, estimating their size, speed, and depth. To confirm, they cross-checked with acoustic recordings in the 5–100 Hz range when whales vocalized near the surface. The low-frequency signals that appeared later, as the whale moved closer to the fiber, matched perfectly. This isn't just about filling a data gap. The technique could also detect toothed whales, which vocalize at frequencies too high for standard DAS. As climate change scrambles marine ecosystems, a tool that tracks whales even when they're silent could be a game-changer for conservation. The research is published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Next step: scaling this up across the global cable network to build a worldwide, always-on whale monitor.
why_it_matters: Tracking whale movements without sound could help protect endangered species as climate change forces them into new, often dangerous territories, and could guide shipping lanes to avoid collisions.

background_read: Svalbard is a remote, icy archipelago in the Norwegian Arctic where climate change is happening faster than in most parts of the world. Whale migration routes are already shifting because of warmer oceans, making real-time tracking more urgent than ever. The global network of submarine fiber-optic cables stretches over 1.3 million kilometers and carries 99% of international data, but scientists are increasingly using these cables as giant sensors for earthquakes and ocean currents. NTNU (the Norwegian University of Science and Technology) is a leading Nordic research university with strong expertise in marine technology and acoustics. Many whale species spend up to 90% of their time in silence, so a tool that can feel their physical presence—like the pressure waves from swimming—offers a powerful new window into their hidden lives.

perspectives.description: Silent detection fills a critical data gap. It could reveal where whales travel and rest, making it easier to create protected zones and reduce ship strikes.
The system only senses whales within about 40 metres of a cable. In the vast ocean, many animals would be missed, and scaling up requires negotiating with cable‑owning telecom companies.

This is part of a broader trend of turning existing infrastructure into environmental sensors. Submarine cables, originally laid for communication, are increasingly used to listen for earthquakes, track storms, and now monitor wildlife.

If a worldwide cable‑based whale monitor becomes reality, it could provide continuous, low‑cost data on marine life. However, it will need international cooperation and significant funding to cross technical and political hurdles.
